nodes.title: SRE and reliability concepts (GCP PCA): Key Ideas
nodes.content: Site Reliability Engineering concepts appear on the GCP PCA exam because Google invented SRE. The exam tests the SLI/SLO/SLA hierarchy, how error budgets translate SLOs into actionable policies, what 'toil' means and why reducing it matters, and the stages of a CI/CD pipeline that reduce deployment risk.

flashcards.front: SLI vs SLO vs SLA — what is each?
flashcards.back: SLI (Service Level Indicator): the metric you actually measure — a real number. Example: '99.2% of homepage requests returned HTTP 200 in < 300 ms over the last 28 days'. SLO (Service Level Objective): the internal reliability target for that SLI. Example: 'SLI must be ≥ 99.9%'. SLA (Service Level Agreement): the contractual commitment to customers, typically weaker than the SLO to provide buffer. Example: 'we guarantee 99.5% availability'. SLI is the measurement; SLO is the goal; SLA is the promise.

flashcards.front: Error budget — what is it and how does it change engineering behavior?
flashcards.back: Error budget = 1 - SLO. If the SLO is 99.9% availability, the error budget is 0.1% — about 43 minutes/month of allowed downtime. While budget remains, engineering teams can deploy risky changes. When budget is nearly exhausted, the team freezes releases and focuses on reliability work. This makes reliability a concrete engineering constraint rather than an abstract goal — developers self-regulate to protect their own ability to ship.

flashcards.front: Toil — what is it in SRE vocabulary and why reduce it?
flashcards.back: Toil is manual, repetitive, automatable work that scales linearly with service growth — on-call responses to known alerts, manual scaling operations, ticket-driven provisioning. SRE teams target keeping toil below 50% of work time. Toil is not the same as overhead (meetings, design docs) — toil specifically has no lasting value beyond getting through the moment. Automating toil frees time for engineering that permanently improves the system.

flashcards.front: CI/CD pipeline stages — what happens at build, test, and deploy?
flashcards.back: Build: compile code, resolve dependencies, create an artifact (container image, JAR, binary) — tagged with commit hash for traceability. Test: unit tests (fast, run every commit), integration tests (service dependencies spun up), end-to-end tests (full stack, slower). Deploy: push artifact to an environment (dev → staging → canary → production), often gated by test results and policy checks. Canary deployment releases to a small traffic percentage first; rollback is fast if error budget spikes.

questions.q: Your team runs a payments API on GKE. You want an availability metric that reflects the ratio of successful requests to total valid requests, so you can define a monthly reliability target for it. In Cloud Monitoring, what should you define first?
choices: A service-level objective (SLO) with a threshold of 99.9%
A service-level indicator (SLI) — good events over valid events
An error budget policy that halts feature launches at 25% burn
An alerting policy on the HTTP 5xx response-code count metric
questions.explanation: SRE defines the SLI first — it is the measurement (successful requests / valid requests). The SLO is a target set on that SLI (e.g., 99.9%), and the error budget derives from the SLO (1 - SLO over the window). You cannot define an SLO without first having an SLI to measure, and alerting policies target metrics, not reliability commitments.

questions.q: Your service has a 99.5% availability SLO measured over a rolling 28-day window. Two weeks in, you have already burned 90% of the error budget from a single incident. Following Google SRE practice, what is the most appropriate next step?
choices: Raise the SLO to 99.9% so the budget accounts for the incident
Continue shipping features to hit quarterly roadmap commitments
Freeze risky feature launches and prioritize reliability work
Add more replicas immediately and mark the incident resolved
questions.explanation: The point of an error budget is to make the reliability-vs-velocity trade explicit. When most of the budget is gone, the on-call SRE guidance is to pause risky changes and invest in reliability work (fixing the class of failure that consumed the budget, hardening rollouts, improving tests). Raising the SLO after the fact hides the miss, blind capacity increases do not address the failure mode, and shipping through a near-empty budget is exactly what the budget is meant to prevent.

questions.q: You need a fully managed Google Cloud pipeline that promotes a container image through dev, staging, and production GKE clusters with approval gates between stages. Which service is designed for this?
choices: Cloud Deploy with a delivery pipeline and targets
Cloud Build with parallel triggers per environment
Artifact Registry remote repositories per environment
Config Sync applying manifests from a Git repository
questions.explanation: Cloud Deploy is Google Cloud's managed continuous-delivery product. A delivery pipeline defines an ordered progression of targets (dev → staging → prod) with optional approval gates, automated promotion, and one-click rollback for GKE, Cloud Run, and GKE Enterprise. Cloud Build handles CI (building/testing the image), Artifact Registry stores the image, and Config Sync applies configuration from Git but does not model a promotion pipeline with gates.

questions.q: You want to release a new revision of a Cloud Run service to 5% of traffic first, then progressively shift more traffic if error rates stay flat. Which built-in Cloud Run capability supports this?
choices: Traffic splitting between revisions with percentage tags
Two separate Cloud Run services fronted by a load balancer
A Cloud Deploy blue/green target with manual promotion
GKE Ingress with weighted backend service routing rules
questions.explanation: Cloud Run supports revision-based traffic splitting natively: each deploy creates a new revision, and you assign any percentage of traffic to any revision (5/95, 25/75, etc.). This is the canonical way to canary a Cloud Run change. Running two services adds needless plumbing, a blue/green target flips 100% at once rather than progressively, and GKE Ingress does not front Cloud Run services.

nodes.title: Software supply-chain security: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Software supply-chain security protects everything that goes into building and delivering software — third-party dependencies, build pipelines, and published artifacts — because attackers increasingly compromise the supply chain instead of the app directly. Exams cover SBOMs, dependency risk, signing and provenance, and pipeline hardening.

flashcards.back: A Software Bill of Materials — a complete inventory of every component, library, and dependency in a piece of software, including versions. It lets you quickly answer 'are we affected?' when a new vulnerability (like Log4Shell) drops, instead of guessing what's inside your builds.

flashcards.front: What are typosquatting and poisoned dependencies?
flashcards.back: Typosquatting publishes a malicious package with a name nearly identical to a popular one (e.g., a one-letter difference), hoping you install it by mistake. A poisoned dependency is a legitimate package that's been compromised to inject malicious code into everyone who pulls it. Both attack you through trusted package ecosystems.

flashcards.front: What do artifact signing and provenance provide?
flashcards.back: Signing (e.g., with Sigstore/cosign) cryptographically proves an artifact came from a trusted publisher and wasn't tampered with. Provenance is verifiable metadata about how and where an artifact was built. Frameworks like SLSA define maturity levels for trustworthy, tamper-resistant build pipelines.

flashcards.front: How do you secure the CI/CD pipeline itself?
flashcards.back: Treat the pipeline as a high-value target: lock down build runners, scope credentials to least privilege and prefer short-lived tokens over stored secrets, pin and verify dependencies, isolate build steps, and require code review. A compromised build server can sign and ship malware as if it were legitimate.

questions.q: A Cloud Build pipeline publishes container images and now needs to sign them so an admission controller can verify their provenance before they run on GKE. Which Google Cloud service produces the attestations?
choices: Cloud Key Management Service creating a signing key
Artifact Registry vulnerability scanning with critical gate
Security Command Center posture policies on the project
Binary Authorization with attestors and signed attestations
questions.explanation: Binary Authorization is the deploy-time gate that only admits images with valid attestations. Attestors verify signatures produced during the build (Cloud Build can create attestations using a KMS-backed key), and the GKE admission controller rejects images that lack them. KMS provides the underlying key material but does not itself model attestations, Artifact Registry scanning finds CVEs (a separate signal), and SCC surfaces posture findings rather than gating admission.

questions.q: You want an alert to fire when your service is consuming its 30-day error budget too quickly — specifically, when the 1-hour burn rate would exhaust the entire budget in less than 5 days if sustained. Which Cloud Monitoring alerting construct fits?
choices: A metric threshold alert on the HTTP 5xx count metric
An uptime check with a 60-second frequency across regions
A log-based metric alert on the string "ERROR" in stderr
An SLO burn-rate alert tied to the service's availability SLO
questions.explanation: Cloud Monitoring exposes SLO burn-rate alerts specifically for this pattern: they fire when the fraction of the error budget being consumed per unit time exceeds a threshold, using a short lookback window for fast detection and often a longer one to suppress noise. Plain 5xx-count thresholds and uptime checks do not know about the SLO or the budget, and a log-based ERROR alert is a symptom trigger unrelated to budget burn.

questions.q: A latency regression appeared in your microservice after a deploy. You want to see, for a single slow request, how much time was spent in each downstream call (auth, database, cache) end-to-end. Which Google Cloud Observability service should you use?
choices: Cloud Logging with a filter on the request's trace ID
Cloud Trace showing a distributed-trace waterfall for the span
Cloud Profiler showing CPU flame graphs by function
Cloud Monitoring dashboard with p99 latency time series
questions.explanation: Cloud Trace is the distributed-tracing product: for a given trace ID it renders a waterfall of spans (auth → DB → cache) with per-span duration — exactly the per-request breakdown you need. Cloud Profiler samples CPU/heap over time by function, not per-request. Cloud Monitoring aggregates latency across requests. Log filtering shows correlated log lines but not a timed span graph.

questions.q: You are updating a GKE Deployment with 12 replicas and want zero downtime. You set strategy.type to RollingUpdate. Which pair of settings caps the number of pods above the desired count and the number of unavailable pods during the roll?
choices: minReadySeconds and progressDeadlineSeconds on the Deployment
revisionHistoryLimit and paused fields on the Deployment spec
maxSurge and maxUnavailable under the RollingUpdate strategy
podDisruptionBudget minAvailable and podAntiAffinity rules set
questions.explanation: Under RollingUpdate, maxSurge caps how many pods above desired can be created during the roll, and maxUnavailable caps how many pods below desired can be unavailable at once — together they govern speed vs safety. minReadySeconds delays marking a pod ready, progressDeadlineSeconds fails the rollout after a timeout, and PodDisruptionBudget protects against voluntary evictions but is not part of the Deployment's rolling strategy itself.

nodes.title: Incident response: Key Ideas
nodes.content: IR follows a documented lifecycle so a panicked 3am pager doesn't turn into 'what do we do now?'. The classic NIST flow is preparation, detection, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned. Exam questions test which phase owns which action.

flashcards.front: NIST IR lifecycle — name the phases.
flashcards.back: (1) Preparation: playbooks, contact lists, hardened images. (2) Detection & Analysis: SIEM alerts, IDS, user reports. (3) Containment: short-term (isolate host) + long-term (block C2 domains). (4) Eradication: remove malware, close vuln. (5) Recovery: restore from clean backup, monitor for re-infection. (6) Lessons learned: post-mortem within 2 weeks, action items tracked.

Short-term: stop the bleed fast — pull the network cable, kill the user session, block the IP. May be reversible. Long-term: durable fix — patch the vuln, rotate creds, deploy IPS rule, sometimes rebuild from scratch. Don't skip short-term: every minute of attacker dwell time multiplies damage.

flashcards.front: Chain of custody — why does it matter?
flashcards.back: If the incident leads to prosecution, evidence must be admissible — every transfer, image, and access logged from acquisition to court. Drives required to be hashed (SHA-256) immediately, copies (not originals) used for analysis, originals stored in a tamper-evident bag with signatures. Skip this and the lawyer dismisses your case.

flashcards.front: What's a post-mortem (lessons learned) supposed to produce?
flashcards.back: Blameless write-up within 2 weeks: timeline, what worked, what didn't, action items with owners + due dates. The goal is process improvement, not punishment — if engineers fear blame they hide details and the next incident is worse. Track action items in your normal sprint board, not in a doc nobody reopens.

questions.q: Your on-call engineer needs to correlate an application log line with the exact request that produced it, across 12 microservices. Which Cloud Logging field, populated automatically when OpenTelemetry propagates context, makes this correlation reliable?
choices: trace field on the LogEntry set to the projects/…/traces/ID form
logging.googleapis.com/spanId set on the LogEntry resource
labels.instance_id derived from the underlying GCE VM identity
resource.type of the LogEntry set to k8s_container consistently
questions.explanation: Setting the LogEntry's trace field to projects/PROJECT/traces/TRACE_ID lets Logs Explorer link straight to the Cloud Trace waterfall for that request, and lets any query filter logs to one request across every service that participated. spanId is useful for a specific span but does not join a request across services on its own, instance_id ties a log to a VM (not a request), and resource.type describes the emitter type rather than the request.

questions.q: During a Sev-1 outage your team is switching between chat, docs, and dashboards. Google SRE practice prescribes named on-call roles so the response stays coordinated. Which role owns the overall incident coordination, delegates work, and communicates status to stakeholders?
choices: Operations Lead running commands and applying fixes hands-on
Communications Lead broadcasting updates to external customers
Planning Lead scheduling the post-incident review and action items
Incident Commander coordinating the response and delegating work
questions.explanation: In Google's incident-management framework the Incident Commander owns coordination — deciding priorities, delegating operational and communications work to the Operations and Communications Leads, and remaining the single point of accountability during the incident. Ops Lead executes remediation, Comms Lead handles stakeholder updates, and a planning role only appears in longer incidents to schedule the postmortem — none of them coordinate the response.

questions.q: You want to identify which functions in a production Go service are consuming the most CPU, sampling continuously in production with negligible overhead. Which Google Cloud Observability service is purpose-built for this?
choices: Cloud Trace to view per-request span durations end-to-end
Cloud Monitoring uptime checks probing the service's endpoint
Cloud Profiler continuously sampling CPU and heap flame graphs
Error Reporting grouping stack traces by frequency of occurrence
questions.explanation: Cloud Profiler is Google Cloud's continuous statistical profiler — it samples CPU, heap, and other resources in production with low overhead and renders flame graphs by function, which is exactly the CPU-hotspot view being asked for. Trace measures per-request latency across services, uptime checks probe availability from outside, and Error Reporting groups exceptions — none of them attribute CPU to functions.

questions.q: Your blameless postmortem template asks for an SRE-specific artefact that lists the concrete work needed to keep the same failure class from recurring, each item assigned to an owner with a due date. What is this called?
choices: The service-level agreement (SLA) attached to the incident
The action items list produced by the postmortem review
The runbook entry created for the on-call rotation to follow
The change-management ticket filed to revert the bad release
questions.explanation: Google's postmortem template treats action items as first-class outputs: each is a concrete, owned, dated piece of follow-up work aimed at preventing recurrence — tracked to closure like any other engineering work. SLAs are contractual promises unrelated to remediation, runbooks are operational guidance rather than a follow-up ledger, and a change-management ticket may or may not exist for a given remediation.
